California has been one of hydrogen’s most enthusiastic supporters for two decades. The state has subsidized hydrogen vehicles, backed refueling networks, supported fuel-cell buses and trucks, invested in hydrogen production and kept the technology prominent in its zero-emission transportation policies. Los Angeles and Long Beach, the two enormous ports that anchor America’s Pacific container trade, have been part of that enthusiasm. So when these ports produce a comprehensive assessment of future marine fuels and leave hydrogen out of their detailed deep-sea shipping plans, it deserves attention well beyond California.

The Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , released in October, is the product of a substantial examination of shipping fleets, carrier preferences, fuel availability and infrastructure costs. The ports recommend developing commercial methanol bunkering demonstrations, continuing existing ship-to-ship LNG bunkering arrangements and avoiding major new fuel terminals until demand becomes credible. Hydrogen, the molecule that California has spent so much money promoting for transportation, did not make the cut for detailed quantitative deep-sea fuel planning.

Supercar ownership has been, and likely always will be, quite a scary proposition for newcomers, save for those who have pockets deep enough to not even care how much the next service or repair bill will cost. However, modern engineering and the cross-platform hardware that exists in many a modern supercar makes ownership a little more approachable compared to the exotics that came before them. For example, classic Ferraris like the F355 and Testarossa require engine-out servicing on an uncomfortably frequent basis, while electrical gremlins, rattling cam chains, and inadequate braking systems trouble the pre-Audi-era Lamborghinis.

Now, look at their modern counterparts. The Ferrari 458 Italia is chain-driven and capable of six-figure mileages, plus its modern DCT transmission is impressively durable and free of pricey clutch changes. Meanwhile, modern Lamborghinis share a lot of hardware with mass-market models from within the Volkswagen-Audi group as well as some other mainstream automakers, which, for buyers that know where to look, brings down servicing and maintenance costs dramatically.

In addition, most come with a couple of small painted dots that almost nobody ever explains. While things like the colored stripes on the tire don't really matter after their initial sale, these dots are key for anyone installing the tire down the road. Here's a quick breakdown of what each dot is and what it signifies.

To be short and sweet, there are typically two dots on a modern tire. First, you'll find a yellow dot. It signifies the lightest part of the tire in question when tested by the manufacturer. Second, a red dot alerts a tire balancer to the point of maximum force variation. Both of those deserve a little unpacking and explanation.

The ever-popular Toyota RAV4 was totally redesigned for the 2026 model year, and for the first time ever it offered exclusively hybridized drivetrains . Considering how momentous that redesign was, one would expect second-year updates to be minimal, and that's mostly the case for the 2027 RAV4, but the handful of updates are good ones. The off-road-oriented RAV4 Woodland becomes slightly more off-road oriented for 2027 with a reworked suspension that adds an inch of ground clearance for a total of 9.1 inches, and all plug-in-hybrid RAV4s, including the RAV4 GR Sport , now feature an NACS port with DC fast-charging abilities and an 11-kW onboard AC charger.

I'm never happy to see prices increase, but at least Toyota has kept the increases to a minimum, with different trim levels costing between $400 and $755 more than they did last year . The cheapest 2027 Toyota RAV4 you can buy is the front-wheel-drive LE trim that now costs $33,895, up $400 from last year, while the cheapest 2027 RAV4 PHEV you can buy is the all-wheel-drive SE that now costs $43,695, which is $600 dearer than last year.

item.dc:creator: Marco Rossi
item.description: A lot of companies build EV models that have an internal-combustion analogue, with the guiding principle of, “the car you liked before, but electric.” There’s a tight thematic cohesiveness to that approach—a BMW i3 and M340i each endeavor to arrive at their optimized level of BMW 3-ness despite the differing powertrains—but the Cadillac Escalade is not like that.

Briefing: A lot of companies build EV models that have an internal-combustion analogue, with the guiding principle of, “the car you liked before, but electric.” There’s a tight thematic cohesiveness to that approach—a BMW i3 and M340i each endeavor to arrive at their optimized level of BMW 3-ness despite the differing powertrains—but the Cadillac Escalade is not like that.

A lot of companies build EV models that have an internal-combustion analogue, with the guiding principle of, “the car you liked before, but electric.” There’s a tight thematic cohesiveness to that approach—a BMW i3 and M340i each endeavor to arrive at their optimized level of BMW 3-ness despite the differing powertrains—but the Cadillac Escalade is not like that. Yes, there are gas and electric versions, but they’re similar only inasmuch as they each avidly pursue the high-level Escalade goals of cosseting bigness and cocky braggadocio. When Tony Soprano got an Escalade in season 5 of The Sopranos , the only question around that casting decision was, what took so long? Today Tony would have more choices in his pursuit of the maximum expression of GM SUV, as do any of us with about $160,000 to spend. Namely, would you rather have a supercharged V-8 Escalade-V or an electric Escalade IQ ?

Cadillac designed the Escalade-V’s exhaust to be extra boisterous , adding a 360-degree loop to the passenger’s-side pipe to equalize the length with the driver’s-side counterpart, for maximum sonic awesomeness. The IQ does not have equal-length dual exhaust. Whatever exhaust it does produce will get you into a tedious and possibly confrontational discussion of well-to-wheel emissions with your uncle at Thanksgiving. However, you’ll never have to worry about thieves stealing your catalytic converters, so I’ll call that one a draw.

Twenty-two full-time riders are entered in the series - but Yamaha is absent in full from the Qatar weekend due to the geopolitical situation, and Pecco Bagnaia was ruled out of the weekend after fracturing his foot in the sprint. Bagnaia will undergo surgery on a pair of metatarsal fractures in his right foot on Monday or Tuesday. Now, Marini has withdrawn from the weekend, too, as he has continued to struggle with fatigue after a viral infection last month. He was able to compete last weekend at Sepang but has laboured from the get-go here, finishing a low-key 13th in the sprint before pulling out following the warm-up. There are questions, too, about whether Maverick Vinales will take the start for Tech3 KTM. A despondent Vinales, who is still not fit after his shoulder injury last year, said he "doesn't want anymore to ride like this". But he did run in the warm-up, and there has been no communication from Tech3 about him sitting out the race. If the grid size ends up at 16, it means Jorge Martin would need to beat just one rider to take the championship fight to Portugal - even if Marc Marquez were to win the grand prix.

Street takeovers are a menace. Heck, the disruptive crime has jurisdictions like Compton installing new medians to prevent takeovers. This, however, isn't that kind of takeover. Twice a year, thousands of snakes take over a small road in Illinois. It's the sort of thing that would be enough to make Indiana Jones ditch his motorcycle, drop his whip, and head for the hills. Now, before you conjure mental images of "Raiders of the Lost Ark" and a writhing tangle of venomous vipers, this is all part of nature. Though there are still thousands of slithery critters on the so-called "Snake Road," a few of which are venomous.

It's enough to shut down the road that runs through part of the Shawnee National Forest in southern Illinois. Every year, the little road closes to vehicle traffic due to the influx of scaly travelers. Not once, but twice every trip around the sun. In fact, it's the only known road in the United States to shut down in observance of a reptile migration. The shutdown isn't meant to protect the national forest's human visitors, either – it's to make sure the road-going snakes can complete their journey unharmed.

If you're into cars, and particularly driving and wrenching on older cars , you'll have doubtless come across old wives' tales about driving and running them. Examples include older vehicles being safer, even though they lack modern safety equipment like airbags, because they're made of thicker steel. Or that filling up with high octane fuel will boost the horsepower of even the most ordinary engine. Both are generally untrue, but what about the one that says leaving a car battery on concrete can damage it?

Like those other two examples, the battery myth is just that. You won't hurt a battery by leaving it on a concrete floor. But also like the safety and octane stories, there's a grain of truth to it. Modern cars are designed to crumple to absorb impacts, and that can make them look less safe after a relatively small accident. And some performance cars, or tuned cars, do deliver more output with higher octane fuel. Which is why, by the same token, even today, you might hear the concrete floor battery warnings repeated by folks who have more experience in looking after cars than you do.

item.dc:creator: Marco Rossi
item.description: The rules surrounding speed limit signs are standard across the country, but how they're followed can vary. The rules, however, are fairly clear. The federal government doesn't set speed limits, even on interstates. Instead, states and local municipalities depend on traffic engineers to help decide posted speed limits.

The rules surrounding speed limit signs are standard across the country, but how they're followed can vary. The rules, however, are fairly clear. The federal government doesn't set speed limits, even on interstates. Instead, states and local municipalities depend on traffic engineers to help decide posted speed limits. Those are determined by considering laws, the areas where the speed limit will be posted, and the safety of the area, including the flow of traffic and frequency of accidents. (Not, though, the long-touted "85th-percentile rule." )

Traffic engineers often refer to their bible, the 1,100-page-plus Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices , written and revised by the Federal Highway Administration. If you're curious, turn to Page 84 of the revised 11th edition, where the section "Speed Limit Signs and Plaques" resides. The item to pay attention to is number 14: "Speed Limit (R2-1) signs, indicating speed limits for which posting is required by law, shall be located at points of change from one speed limit to another."

If you look at the lineage of Aston Martin's main production grand tourer over the years, it goes straight from the DB9 of the 2000s and early 2010s to the DB11 in 2016. Why did they seemingly just skip DB10? Is the number 10 unlucky in British culture? Turns out, A) it didn't and B) no. In fact, Aston Martin did indeed build a DB10; it just never made production.

A few years before the DB11 came along, work was underway on Daniel Craig's fourth James Bond movie, "Spectre." Director Sam Mendes, who helmed the wildly successful and, by most accounts, very good "Skyfall," was returning, and he wanted a new Aston Martin for Bond to drive. Enter the DB10, a car that was originally a concept sketch for the next Vantage , but became its own special model brought to life specifically for the movie. Fun fact: this was apparently the very first time an entirely new car was made for a Bond film.

Getting pulled over is never a fun time. The reasons are seemingly endless, from driving a police magnet to dangling a keepsake from the rearview mirror or having Flock misidentify your car as stolen . Now imagine going through any of these scenarios while also having a disability that creates communication challenges, such as autism. For someone with sensory, cognitive, and verbal difficulties, the already stressful event of being pulled over could lead to trauma or even being shot. And for the police officer, being unaware of the driver's medical condition can lead to miscommunication and mishandling of the situation.

That's why the Blue Envelope Program was developed: to improve communication between law enforcement and people who require additional accommodations or time during stops. Designed to be an all-inclusive information tool that's easy and straightforward to use for both the driver and officer, on the envelope's exterior are printed instructions and guidelines regarding how to interact with one another, while inside are essential documents, such as a driver's license, proof of insurance, and vehicle registration.

It's probably been two decades since you've used a floppy disk — unless you're managing air traffic or preparing to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. The Federal Aviation Administration, a bit behind the technology curve, announced Thursday that it will finally phase out 3.5-inch floppy disks at air traffic control facilities. The agency aims to rid itself of the antiquated technology by the end of 2028. In its place, air traffic controllers will have a modern, fully digitized system at their disposal.

The FAA plans to replace four legacy systems that date back to the 1980s with the Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) at 435 locations. The transition has already happened at Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and a pair of data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. These older systems were simply no longer sustainable to operate. Air traffic control currently depends, in part, on Compaq computers running on Windows 95. Let's be honest, talking about cars being software-defined still feels rather alien — after all, it wasn't all that long ago when all you needed was gas and a license to get going on the open road. But today's cars are becoming more like a smartphone. One day, you don't have a feature; then a software update happens overnight, and bingo, you have it!

Or, in some cases, you can't drive your car until it finishes its software update, much like you can't scroll through cat videos on Instagram until the app finishes updating. We've seen stories where modern cars are potentially losing features thanks to a lack of software support . If you've been feeling that way, you're not alone. Our cars are becoming increasingly reliant on lines of code rather than physical components to control what, how, and when they can do things. Simply put, they're becoming software-defined vehicles.

Lando Norris snatched a stunning Brazilian Grand Prix pole position at Interlagos in torrential rain, as George Russell felt Mercedes robbed him of a chance to finish first, despite a five-place grid penalty rendering that effectively irrelevant anyway. After rain delayed the start of F1 qualifying by an hour and 25 minutes, Q1 got underway and you could tell conditions were treacherous merely by the rarely used wet weather tyres being bolted onto all of the cars, while by the time Q3 rolled around it was dry enough for intermediates. But, and it was a big but, the weather radar suggested there would only be time for one flying lap before more heavy rain arrived early in Q3. In the end there was time for two laps, and Russell was fastest with the first, and then looked good enough to be quickest in the second before backing off at the end of his second lap when he caught Alex Albon's Williams.

GR: "Move, Albono!" Merc: “So, we will get one more lap here.” Russell: “You need to tell me mate what I’m doing, if I’m backing or going.” Merc: “We can back up now, back up now.” Russell: “Are you sure?” Merc: “It’s raining heavier now.” [Russell prepares to start final lap] Merc: “It’s raining heavily now in the pitlane.” Russell: “Mate I should have f***ing finished the lap!” [Halfway round lap when it’s clear it’s done] Russell: “MATE! You f***ing told me to back off. What the hell!” Wolff: “George you’re P2" Russell: “Yeah but…P2. I don’t wanna be P2, I want to be P1. That was a P1 lap. F******ing hell!” The final gap was 0.204s, but it doesn't really matter as Russell will drop back five places for an engine penalty.

We all knew this day was coming, but none of us wanted to face it; the MkV Toyota Supra and G29 BMW Z4 are officially off the new car market. Our friends at CarsDirect analyzed national dealer inventory data on Tuesday and found that there are no more new Supras or Z4s on dealer lots across the United States. Both models were built at the Magna Steyr contract manufacturing facility in Austria, but their production run concluded in spring of this year. At least both manufacturers commemorated the end of production with Final Editions, but we're still sad to see both nameplates join the great new car lot in the sky. For now, at least.

Toyota Motor North America's senior vice president of product planning and strategy Cooper Ericksen told MotorTrend that a Supra successor is coming, but that there will be another hiatus in the iconic sports car's legacy. Ericksen said, "it is our goal to have a gap that is significantly less [than the last one]." That last gap between the fourth-generation Supra and the fifth-generation car lasted an excruciating 20 years, so hopefully the sixth-generation Supra comes much sooner than that. Sadly BMW has not publicly announced plans for a fourth-generation Z4 as of now.

Here's the reason to even posit this: Carmakers want a cheaper way to build hybrids, EVs, and gas cars on the same platform and on the same assembly line. Adding or subtracting parts will make that too costly — which may result in them just ditching any manual effort, if that's the only solution.

Now that you understand the why of this reporting, we'll also acknowledge why some readers are freaking out about the fact that the 12Cilindri Manuale will simulate the experience of shifting. It's not a conventional manual, and we'll explain how it works in greater depth, but the gist is that Ferrari's linking an electric stalk and faux clutch pedal to an eight-speed dual-clutch drivetrain. It's as real (or fake) as paddle shifters, just via a dongle and pedal.

School buses haven't changed much since 1939 , but they came a long way before then. Some of the first vehicles used to take kids to school were simply horse-drawn wagons. It wasn't until the start of World War I that the first motorized buses seem to have appeared in this country. That's when a company called Wayne Works introduced a model in 1914. It was built on a long-wheelbase Model T chassis, so its engine was in the traditional location, under the hood up front.

Fast-forward a few years and we find Crown Coach evolving the concept of motorized school buses even further. Crown was a major commercial-vehicle manufacturer, founded in 1903 to sell business wagons to businessmen. It would survive all the way up to 1990 by building not only buses, but also hearses, fire trucks, bakery trucks, ambulances, and even airplanes.

Brazilian Grand Prix F1 2026 qualifying has been red flagged barely two minutes in for horrendous wet weather conditions. Rain was always a possibility and was forecast for Saturday at Interlagos, but torrential rain even as the session got underway caught out a host of cars and forced Formula 1 stewards into action. Eight cars: Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes, George Russell's Mercedes, Charles Leclerc's Ferrari, Isack Hadjar's Red Bull, the Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto, Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin and the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas all ventured out on intermediate tyres, but almost as soon as the cars hit the track it became clear that the conditions weren't driveable. Replays showed Lando Norris almost crashing, and Antonelli and Hadjar both laughed at how ridiculous the conditions were, also expressing the need for waterproofs.

Gabriel Bortoleto summed up the mood: "When I get out, I need to change my clothes, I'm completely wet!" Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton appeared to demonstrate their experience in F1 by not venturing out on track and remaining dry in the garage. There's no confirmed restart time yet as rain continues to pummel the track. Nico Hulkenberg was told the rain would fall this heavily for at least 10 minutes, with that radio message coming at 1808 UK time.

The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane is capable of flying 2,193.2 mph with a ceiling above 85,000 feet. To achieve those feats, it packed a pair of Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets to enjoy a combined 50,000 pounds of thrust, and it even used a new kind of fuel that could withstand the friction from those blistering speeds. However, getting those mighty motors to turn over in the first place was no simple task, which is where the Buick Nailhead comes into play. It might not have directly powered the plane, but its earliest flights were only possible thanks to the engine.

A turbine engine requires a certain amount of airflow to ensure the fuel first ignites properly, and it has to reach a certain speed before the combustion process can sustain itself. As a result, the turbojet engines need to begin spinning even before they're operating on their own. But these are massive mills weighing in at 6,000 pounds each, so a simple electric starter like the one in a traditional car wouldn't have the strength to get the job done. A pair of Buick engines, on the other hand, would be enough to give its turbines the power they needed.

Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance.

A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

For any savvy driver reluctant to cough up the eye-wateringly steep new-car asking prices today, a used car seems like a no-brainer option. However, buying a used car can be a minefield, too. Inspect the car too casually, and you could be flirting with unreliability. Luckily, the non-profit organization Consumer Reports (CR) helps buyers identify the vehicles that are much more likely to suffer unexpected faults or hidden issues — like burning oil in the case of gas-powered cars.

For those wondering, your car burning oil means oil is getting into the combustion chamber where it gets burned along with the air-fuel mixture. And since oil is essential for lubrication, cooling, and protecting the internal components inside the engine, your car burning or using too much oil can have serious consequences for its longevity. Naturally, this problem will cause oil levels to run low, reducing the lubrication inside the engine — also known as oil starvation . Without an effective lubrication film, the friction between moving parts inside the engine can accelerate wear on critical components, which can ultimately result in complete engine failure.

It's also still genuinely affordable, making it one of the cheaper alternatives to Japanese performance cars that have skyrocketed in value .

But perhaps the main reason for its celebrated status is its engine: Nissan's VQ35. In essence, it's a 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6 that produces around 287 horsepower in early 350Zs (or closer to 300 hp in the Nismo versions). Even by today's standards, the 350Z is quick: in Car and Driver 's testing, 0 to 60 miles per hour took 5.4 seconds, and it didn't top out until 156 mph.
